description: We are a team of 15-year-old high school students passionate about gaming and space, and we built Twelve Minutes Out to unite both. Rather than guessing, we grounded our entire simulation in real NASA data: JPL ephemeris orbital mechanics, Perseverance rover Jezero Crater weather telemetry, and official NASA-STD-3001 human life-support thresholds. It’s an authentic, high-stakes mission control experience powered by real-world spaceflight physics and science!
summary:
Twelve Minutes Out is a hard-science fiction mission control simulation where you manage a Martian crew separated from Earth by a relentless 24-minute round-trip communication delay. When emergencies strike—such as hull breaches, solar radiation spikes, or life-support failures—the crew is entirely on their own for the first 12 minutes, and any guidance you transmit takes another 12 minutes to reach them.

Grounded in peer-reviewed aerospace data rather than fictional techno-babble, every threat and system constraint is modeled after real spaceflight standards:

Orbital Mechanics: Trajectory calculations use real JPL ephemeris math to simulate Hohmann transfer windows and changing light-time delays.

Martian Weather: Dust storms, pressure drops, and thermal shifts replicate telemetry from NASA’s Perseverance rover at Jezero Crater.

Radiation & Health: Solar particle events follow Curiosity RAD baselines, while life-support limits strictly obey official NASA-STD-3001 human health standards.

Gameplay balances immediate crisis response—queueing diagnostic patches and watching automated AI protocols unfold—with long-term survival logistics. You must triage medical emergencies, ration power across dust-covered solar arrays, and guide high-latency EVA repairs across a grueling 500-day deployment at Ares Station Alpha, turning real physics into a gripping test of leadership under extreme isolation.
details:
Twelve Minutes Out is a hard-science fiction, real-time mission control simulation game where players manage a Martian crew facing a brutal reality: a 24-minute round-trip communication delay with Earth.

  • What it does & how it works: Players act as mission control supervisors managing Ares Station Alpha on Mars. Because of light-speed lag, radio signals take 12 minutes one-way. When crises like hull breaches or solar radiation spikes occur, the crew is entirely on their own for the first 12 minutes, and any commands sent take another 12 minutes to arrive. Players must navigate this lag by queueing autonomous protocols, coordinating high-latency EVAs, and balancing power and medical resources.
  • Benefits & Intended Impact: The project bridges entertainment and hard science, educating players on orbital mechanics, planetary weather, and human spaceflight constraints while delivering a deeply tense, immersive strategy experience.
  • Tools, Languages & Tech: While specific code repositories aren't listed, the simulation relies heavily on authentic real-world frameworks, including JPL ephemeris math for orbital trajectories, Perseverance rover MEDA telemetry for Martian weather, Curiosity RAD data for radiation tracking, and NASA-STD-3001 standards for life-support systems.
  • Creativity & Considerations: The game's core creativity stems from weaponizing time delay as a central mechanic rather than hiding it behind instant sci-fi communication. The team carefully balanced historical and scientific accuracy—avoiding fictional techno-babble—with engaging gameplay loops, ensuring every environmental hazard, radiation spike, and physiological threshold reflects true aerospace engineering challenges.
dataRefs: Real Earth → Mars trajectory (Mars Science Laboratory, 2011–2012)
Radiation measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument (cruise and Mars surface)
Mars weather at Jezero crater during the January 2022 dust event
Real heartbeat shape (ECG) from a healthy adult
Caution and critical limits (NASA crew health standard)
How much oxygen one astronaut uses and how much CO₂ they breathe out
Mars terrain height map (MOLA laser altimeter)
